title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values level by level but from the bottom level up to the root, left to right within each level.
shortTitle: Reverse Level Order Traversal (Bottom-up Level Order)

s1_definition.profdef: Perform a standard Tree BFS collecting each level's values, but insert each completed level at the front of the result (or reverse the result at the end). The traversal itself is unchanged; only the accumulation order differs.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants its approval chart printed clerks-first, then department heads, then the branch manager at the very bottom of the printout. You still gather staff rank by rank from the top, but you stack each gathered rank on top of the previous so the last rank gathered prints first.
s1_definition.oneliner: Do normal level-order BFS, but add each level to the front of the result so the bottom level comes out first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Perform a standard Tree BFS collecting each level's values, but insert each completed level at the front of the result (or reverse the result at the end). The traversal itself is unchanged; only the accumulation order differs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants its approval chart printed clerks-first, then department heads, then the branch manager at the very bottom of the printout. You still gather staff rank by rank from the top, but you stack each gathered rank on top of the previous so the last rank gathered prints first.

**One line to remember:** Do normal level-order BFS, but add each level to the front of the result so the bottom level comes out first.

sections.s2_technical:
The queue-based BFS with the level-size snapshot is identical to top-down level order. The only change is where each finished level goes. Using a `LinkedList` as the result and calling `result.addFirst(level)` places the most recently completed (lower) level ahead of the earlier (higher) ones, so after processing, the bottom level is first and the root's level is last. Alternatively collect top-down and reverse once at the end.

For example the tree with levels [1], [2,3], [4,5,6] yields [[4,5,6],[2,3],[1]]. Using `addFirst` avoids a separate reversal pass and keeps the logic in one loop.

A senior-level nuance is the data structure choice: `LinkedList.addFirst` is O(1), so prepending each level is cheap, whereas `ArrayList.add(0, x)` would be O(n) per insert because it shifts elements. Picking the deque-backed list is the small detail that keeps the whole operation linear rather than quadratic.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India produces an approval chart for an audit report that must read from the ground up, listing the lowest-level approvers first and the branch head last, matching how escalations flow upward. The tree is traversed top-down naturally, so the system must flip the level ordering without flipping within each level. This is exactly reverse level order: BFS as usual, but prepend each level.

The code contains an `AuditNode`, an `EscalationChart` with `bottomUpLevels(root)`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: tree root 1, children 2 and 3, leaves 4,5 under 2 and 6 under 3.

Step 1: Queue [1]. Drain level [1], enqueue 2,3. addFirst makes result [[1]].

Step 2: Drain level [2,3], enqueue 4,5,6. addFirst makes result [[2,3],[1]].

Step 3: Drain level [4,5,6]. addFirst makes result [[4,5,6],[2,3],[1]].

Step 4: Final result is [[4,5,6],[2,3],[1]], bottom level first.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Bottom-up escalation chart: [[4, 5, 6], [2, 3], [1]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: tree rooted at 1
    │
    ▼
  EscalationChart.bottomUpLevels()  (queue + addFirst)
    │ level[1]     → result=[[1]]
    │ level[2,3]   → result=[[2,3],[1]]
    │ level[4,5,6] → result=[[4,5,6],[2,3],[1]]
    ▼
  Output: [[4,5,6],[2,3],[1]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reverse level order traversal is ordinary top-down level-order BFS with a single change in how I accumulate results. I still process the tree with a FIFO queue and the level-size snapshot, draining exactly one level at a time and enqueuing children, but instead of appending each finished level I prepend it to the front of the result. Because the bottom level is completed last, prepending puts it first, so the final structure reads from the ground up while each level internally stays left to right.

The one detail I call out is the data structure: I use a linked-list-backed deque so that prepending a level is a constant-time operation, because using an array list and inserting at index zero would shift all existing levels on every insert and quietly turn a linear algorithm into a quadratic one.

In my work at the National Bank of India this produced an audit escalation chart that had to read from the lowest approvers up to the branch head, mirroring how escalations travel upward. The tree was naturally traversed top-down, so I ran the standard BFS and prepended each completed level, which gave the bottom-up ordering without reversing within any level and without a second pass over the data.
